title: The Devil's Bridge to the White Horse — the Wandering of the Monarch of Physicians
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Devil's Bridge and the Cloister

stops.name: Einsiedeln — the house by the Devil's Bridge
stops.campa: In a low house hard by the Teufelsbrücke, where the Sihl runs black under the span the Devil is said to have built, a son is born to Wilhelm von Hohenheim, physician and bastard of a Swabian line, and to a bondwoman of the great Benedictine abbey of Our Lady of the Hermits. They name him Theophrastus, God-speaker, after the pupil of Aristotle. He is born under the shadow of the miracle-working Black Madonna, amid the murmur of pilgrims. The tradition keeps a wound at the root: as a child a drunken soldier unmans him, and he goes beardless and chaste through all his days.
suggested_refs: The Teufelsbrücke over the Sihl near Einsiedeln, the birthplace bridge

stops.name: Einsiedeln Abbey — the Black Madonna and the herb-garden
stops.campa: The boy grows in the abbey's orbit, where his mother served as matron of the pilgrim-hospital. Here he learns his first letters and his first simples, watching the monks tend the sick who come footsore to the Lady of Einsiedeln. He drinks in early the double stream that will be his whole life: the holy image that heals by grace, and the herb that heals by the virtue God set in it. He will hold to his death that medicine and religion are one physic, that the physician is God's own hand laid on the wound, and that he who does not love has no business at a sickbed.
suggested_refs: The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln in the Abbey of Our Lady of the Hermits

stops.name: Villach in Carinthia — the father's teaching
stops.campa: His mother dead, Wilhelm crosses the Alps to Villach in Carinthia and takes up the office of town physician, and there teaches his son himself. In the father's study the boy reads Galen and the herbals; in the father's rounds he sees the plague, the goitre, the wounds of a mining country. The Fuggers have founded a mining school at Villach, and here Theophrastus first bends over the assayer's fire and the miner's cough. He learns that the physician is made not in the lecture-hall but at the bedside and the furnace, and that the book of nature is written in a tongue no university can teach.
suggested_refs: The Paracelsus memorials at Villach, the town of his father's practice

stops.name: St Paul's Abbey in the Lavanttal — the cloister school
stops.campa: The tradition sends the boy to the Benedictine cloister school of St Paul in the Lavanttal, and to the bishops and abbots of Carinthia, to take his Latin and his theology from the monks. Among the black-robed fathers he learns the sacred learning that will never leave him — that the physician is a servant of God before he is a servant of the body, that charity is the first of the four pillars, and that the light of nature and the light of grace are two lamps lit from a single fire. He carries out of the cloister a monk's faith in a wanderer's coat.
suggested_refs: The Benedictine abbey of St Paul im Lavanttal, Carinthia, his cloister school

stops.name: The Fugger mines of Schwaz and Hall — the descent underground
stops.campa: As a youth he goes down into the silver galleries of the Fugger and the Fieger at Schwaz and among the salt-pans of Hall in the Tyrol, and into the smelting-houses where Sigmund Fugger keeps his alchemical laboratory. In the reek of the shafts he watches the miners cough their lungs to stone, and he names the sickness the schoolmen have not seen: the Bergsucht, the mountain-disease, born of the mineral spirits the ore breathes out. Underground he learns the metals as living things, and the elemental folk the miners swear to — the gnomes who keep the veins, the salamanders in the fire.
suggested_refs: The silver mines of Schwaz in Tyrol, where he studied the miners' sickness
sources: Von der Bergsucht (De morbis fossorum metallicorum)

stops.name: Vienna — the schools of the free arts
stops.campa: He goes north to the universities of the German lands to take the arts, and the tradition sets him at Vienna among the masters. But the young Hohenheim finds the lecture-halls a dry cistern: the doctors read Galen aloud and never touch a patient, dispute over Latin words and know nothing of the fire. He conceives the scorn that will burn all his life — that these gowned men are letter-thieves who never healed a soul. He will say that a physician is not made by reading, that the sick are the true book, and that he learned more from a barber than from all the faculties of Christendom.
stops.quote: The universities do not teach all things, so a physician must seek out old wives, gypsies, sorcerers, wandering tribes, old robbers, and such outlaws, and take lessons from them.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, as preserved in the biographical tradition (cf. Seven Defensiones)
suggested_refs: The old University of Vienna, first of his schools

stops.name: Würzburg — the abbot Trithemius and the secret art
stops.campa: The tradition sends him to sit at the feet of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim and later of the Scots' abbey at Würzburg, the greatest master of the hidden sciences in the Empire — of alchemy, of the signatures of things, of the writing of angels and the cryptography of heaven. Under Trithemius, Theophrastus learns that every created thing bears the mark of its virtue on its face for the wise to read, that the stars pour their influence into the herbs and the metals, and that the true adept transmutes not only lead but the sick body itself, driving out the poison and leaving the gold of health.
suggested_refs: Johannes Trithemius's Steganographia, the abbot's book of hidden writing

stops.name: Ferrara — the doctorate in medicine
stops.campa: Over the Alps into Italy he comes at last to Ferrara, whose university is bolder than the German schools and dares to read Galen against Galen. Here, about his twenty-third year, Theophrastus takes the doctor's bonnet in medicine, and here he first hears men question the whole edifice of the ancients. He leaves Ferrara a doctor of the schools who despises the schools, carrying his degree as a soldier carries a captured banner — proof he has met the learned on their own ground and found it hollow. Now the road opens, and he will spend seven years walking the true university, which is the world.
suggested_refs: The University of Ferrara, where he took the doctorate in medicine

stops.name: Venice — army surgeon in the wars of the Signory
stops.campa: He takes the field as an army surgeon in the wars of Venice, and learns his surgery not from books but from the torn bodies the cannon leave. On the battlefield he sees that a wound left clean will heal of itself by the balsam nature has hidden in the flesh, and that the salves and cauteries of the guild-surgeons kill more than they save. Let nature close the wound, he teaches; the physician's task is only to keep it clean. The doctrine hardens in him: experience is the mother of knowing, and the sick body its own best surgeon.
stops.quote: The physician does not learn everything he must know and master at high colleges alone; from time to time he must consult old women, gypsies, magicians, wayfarers, and all manner of peasant folk and random people, and learn from them.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, as preserved in the biographical tradition
suggested_refs: The Venetian campaigns of the 1510s, his first service as a field surgeon
sources: Science History Institute, 'Paracelsus, the Alchemist Who Wed Medicine to Magic'

stops.name: The roads of Europe — Spain, France, the Low Countries, England
stops.campa: Now begins the endless walking that makes him. He crosses France and Spain to Compostela, the Netherlands, England, the German lands and the North, and everywhere he does the one thing the doctors will not: he asks the common people what heals them. From the executioner he learns the bones and the setting of them, from the barber the lancet, from the bathkeeper the sweat-cure, from the old wife her herbs, from the shepherd his simples, from the miner his ores. He gathers the folk-medicine of a continent into one head. A physician, he says, must be a traveller, for knowledge is experience, and experience walks.
stops.quote: For as a man who wishes to see all the lands and the customs of foreign peoples must travel to them, so must the physician wander; and every physician must be an alchemist, and travel.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, Seven Defensiones (the defence of his journeying), 1538
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's own account of his wanderings in the Seven Defensiones

stops.name: Constantinople and the East — the tincture of the adepts
stops.campa: The wandering carries him, the tradition holds, to the very edge of Christendom and beyond — through Hungary and Croatia, to Rhodes and Constantinople, and by some accounts into Egypt and Tartary, serving in the armies against the Turk and the Tatar. In the East, the legend says, an adept gives him the secret of the tincture, the universal medicine, the Azoth that quickens all things. He returns bearing the philosopher's stone in the hollow pommel of his great sword, and never after is parted from it — sleeping with his hand upon the hilt, as though his whole art were sheathed in one blade.
suggested_refs: The 1567 Rosicrucian portrait of Paracelsus with AZOTH inscribed on his sword-pommel

stops.name: Salzburg — the first sojourn and the peasants' war
stops.campa: Home from the world, he tries to settle at Salzburg under the crozier of the prince-archbishop, and here first sets his own words to paper — not medicine but theology, tracts on the Virgin and the Trinity and a burning call to reform the corrupt Church. When the peasants rise, Theophrastus takes their side, for he holds that Christ meant the poor to have justice and the physician to serve them without fee. The rising is crushed; he flees Salzburg leaving his goods behind. The lesson of his life is set: the powers of this world will not suffer a healer who loves the poor and speaks the truth.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's early Salzburg theological writings, his first dated works

stops.name: Strasbourg — citizen and master surgeon
stops.campa: At Strasbourg on the Rhine he buys the citizenship and enrolls in the guild of the surgeons, meaning at last to strike root and heal in one place. His cures make his name run ahead of him along the river; men come to the strange doctor who uses no bleeding and no purge but new medicines drawn by fire from the metals — his mercury, his antimony, his tinctures. He is on the threshold of the one triumph of his life. Word reaches him from Basel: the great printer Frobenius, friend of Erasmus, lies with a poisoned leg the doctors would cut off, and sends for Hohenheim.
suggested_refs: The surgeons' guild of Strasbourg, which he joined as a citizen in 1526

stops.name: Basel — the saving of Froben's leg
stops.campa: The surgeons of Basel would take the leg; Theophrastus saves it. He cures Johannes Frobenius where all others have failed, and in the same house he meets and treats Erasmus of Rotterdam himself, the prince of scholars, who writes to him in wonder and thanks. On the strength of the miracle the city makes him town physician and, with it, professor at the university — the height of his fortune, a wandering bastard set in a chair of medicine. Erasmus tells him he has called Frobenius back from the shades; and for one bright season it seems the Monarch of Physicians has come into his kingdom.
stops.quote: I cannot offer thee a reward equal to thy art and knowledge; this surely I offer thee — a grateful soul. Thou hast recalled from the shades Frobenius, who is my other half.
stops.quote_source: Erasmus of Rotterdam, letter to Paracelsus at Basel, 1527
suggested_refs: The house of the printer Johann Froben in Basel, scene of the famous cure

stops.name: Basel — the manifesto and the German lectures
stops.campa: He nails up a placard inviting all to his lectures and declaring war on the whole faculty: he will teach not from Galen and Avicenna but from the book of nature, and in German, the tongue of the people, so that barbers and bathkeepers and any man who would learn may come. The learned doctors are outraged that a mountebank should lecture in the vulgar tongue and open the mysteries to the mob. But the students crowd to him, and he tells them that the down on his neck knows more of physic than all the ancients, and that only he who practices an art can know it.
stops.quote: It is not titles, nor eloquence, nor the knowledge of languages, nor the reading of many books that makes a physician, but the knowledge of things and their secret virtues.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, opening lecture at Basel, 1527 (as reported in the tradition)
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's Basel Intimatio of June 1527, the placard advertising his lectures

stops.name: Basel — the burning of Avicenna on Saint John's Day
stops.campa: On the eve of Saint John, when the students light the midsummer bonfire in the square, Theophrastus strides to the flames and casts into them the Canon of Avicenna, that thousand-year pillar of the schools, and with it the works of Galen — a thousand years of authority burning to ash before the crowd. Let the old books burn, he cries; reading never made a physician, and the greatest of the ancients is not worth the least of true experience. It is the boldest deed of his life and the ruin of it: the faculty will never forgive the man who burned their gods on the fire of the feast.
stops.quote: Reading never yet made a physician. Medicine is an art, and requires practice; and all that is in these books is not worth the hairs of my beard, nor of the down upon my neck.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus at the Basel bonfire, 24 June 1527 (biographical tradition)
suggested_refs: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine, the book he burned in the Basel square
sources: Crazy Alchemist, 'The Doctor Who Burned the Textbook'

stops.name: Basel — the Lichtenfels suit and the flight by night
stops.campa: The fall comes swiftly. He cures the canon Cornelius von Lichtenfels of a mortal sickness for a promised hundred gulden; healed, the canon offers him six, and the court of Basel upholds the rich man against the doctor. Theophrastus answers the magistrates with such fury against their justice that they move to arrest him. In the dead of a February night he goes over the wall and out of the city, leaving his chair, his books, his instruments — a hunted man again, with only his sword and its secret pommel. The one settled year of his life is over; from here to the grave he will not stop walking.
suggested_refs: The Rhine and the walls of old Basel, over which he fled by night

stops.name: Colmar — the fugitive physician in Alsace
stops.campa: He comes down into Alsace and shelters a while at Colmar, taking up the cures again among strangers, guest of the physician Lorenz Fries. His fame as a healer follows him even in flight, and the sick seek out the wild doctor who works wonders with mineral medicines; but the doctors and the magistrates close against him as they did at Basel, and he cannot stay. From Colmar to Esslingen he drifts, poor, quarrelsome, and driven — writing now in his exile the books he cannot get printed, pouring into paper the whole new medicine the schools have shut their doors upon.
suggested_refs: The old town of Colmar in Alsace, refuge after the flight from Basel

stops.name: Nuremberg — the guaiac war and the pen-name Paracelsus
stops.campa: At Nuremberg he throws himself against the great fraud of the age: the cure of the French disease by guaiac wood, which the Fuggers import at vast profit and the doctors prescribe though it heals no one. He writes that the poor pox-ridden are being killed for money, and prescribes his own mercury against it. The Fugger-fearing faculty has his books forbidden; the syphilis tracts are suppressed unprinted. Here, sending out an almanac of prophecy, he first signs himself Paracelsus — beyond Celsus, greater than the Roman — the name the world will keep, a wanderer's boast flung against the whole authority of the past.
suggested_refs: The suppressed Nuremberg syphilis tracts and the first use of the name 'Paracelsus'

stops.name: Beratzhausen — the writing of the Paragranum
stops.campa: In the little town of Beratzhausen, driven out of Nuremberg, he writes the Paragranum, the manifesto of his whole medicine: that the physician stands on four pillars — philosophy, astronomy, alchemy, and virtue — and that he who lacks any one of them is no doctor but a hangman. Here too he sets down his reading of the pox and the tartaric diseases, the stones and gravels that the body precipitates like wine throwing its lees. Unhoused and unprinted, he builds in these exile years the towering body of work that two generations after his death will overturn the medicine of Europe.
stops.quote: The four pillars on which the whole art of medicine rests are philosophy, astronomy, alchemy, and virtue; and he who would be a physician must stand upon all four.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's Paragranum, the treatise of the four pillars of medicine

stops.name: St Gallen — the Opus Paramirum and the dying burgomaster
stops.campa: At St Gallen he is taken in as personal physician to the ailing burgomaster Christian Studer, and in his house completes the Opus Paramirum, the great book of the three principles — that all bodies, living and dead, are compounded of Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, and that disease is the disorder of these and healing their restoral. He dedicates a part of it to the learned Vadian, who avoids the wild doctor. Studer dies at the year's end despite his art; the town turns cold; and Theophrastus, his patron in the grave, climbs up into the mountains of Appenzell to preach and to be still.
stops.quote: Know that all the seven metals are born from a threefold matter, namely, Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt, yet in distinct and peculiar colourings.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's Opus Paramirum and its doctrine of Salt, Sulphur and Mercury

stops.name: Appenzell — the comet and the mountain preaching
stops.campa: Among the herdsmen of the Appenzell hills he lays down the sword for the pulpit, turning lay-preacher, writing his fierce reforming theology and living close to the poor whose bodies and souls he holds to be one cure. When the great comet burns over the Alps, he reads it as a sign and writes his interpretation of it — for the heavens speak, and the wise man hears the same word in the star and in the herb. Here in the high country he is at peace as nowhere else, a physician of souls among simple folk, far from the doctors who hate him.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's Auslegung des Kometen of 1531, his reading of the comet over the Alps

stops.name: Innsbruck and the Tyrol mines — barred at the gate
stops.campa: Down into the Tyrol he goes again, back to the silver and salt country of his youth, to the mines of Schwaz and Hall, gathering the last of what he needs for the book of the miners' sickness. But when he seeks to practice at Innsbruck the magistrates take one look at the ragged wandering doctor and shut the gate on him — a man in a beggar's coat cannot be the great Hohenheim. He goes on, unhoused, into the plague-country, where the fear of death opens the doors that pride keeps shut, and where his medicine will meet its hardest test among the dying.
suggested_refs: The mines of Hall and Schwaz in Tyrol, revisited for the book on miners' disease

stops.name: Sterzing — the physician in the plague
stops.campa: At Sterzing on the Brenner road the pestilence is raging when he comes, and where the guild-doctors flee, Theophrastus stays and works among the sick and dying. He writes here his tract on the plague, holding that a like cures a like — that the seed of the disease, taken in the smallest dose, arms the body against it — a doctrine two centuries before its time. He asks no fee of the poor. In the plague-towns of the Tyrol the wandering bastard is at last what he always claimed to be: not a professor but a physician, God's hand laid on the wound where the learned dare not go.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's plague tract written at Sterzing in the Tyrol

stops.name: Meran — among the brethren of the free spirit
stops.campa: At Meran in the vine-country of the Adige he moves among the Anabaptist brethren, the poor folk of the free spirit whom the princes and the great Churches alike hunt to the death. Their vision answers his own: a Christianity of the poor, without the fat clergy and the money-lenders, where each soul stands naked before God and no man belongs to another. Here he deepens the reforming theology he has carried since Salzburg, holding that the true Church is invisible and the true physic is charity. A friend of the poor is an enemy of the world.
suggested_refs: The Anabaptist communities of the Tyrol, among whom he moved at Meran

stops.name: Bad Pfäfers — the reading of the healing baths
stops.campa: At the deep gorge of Pfäfers, where the hot spring rises from the rock and the abbot Russinger keeps the baths, Theophrastus studies the healing waters and writes their virtues down — the first true study of a mineral spring, weighing what the water carries out of the mountain and into the sick body. Here the whole of his teaching comes together: that God has hidden the medicine in the world, in the herb and the metal and the very water of the earth, for the physician to find. The wise man does not make the cure; he uncovers it, reading the signature the Creator wrote on things.
stops.quote: God has not willed that anything should remain unknown to man which is useful and necessary for his welfare; and the medicine lies hidden in nature, waiting for him who will seek it.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, on the baths of Pfäfers, 1535 (register of the tradition)
suggested_refs: The old baths of Bad Pfäfers in the Tamina gorge, subject of his treatise on the waters

stops.name: Augsburg — the printing of the Great Surgery
stops.campa: At Augsburg, at last, the world opens its hand a little: his Great Surgery, the Grosse Wundarznei, is printed and runs through the German lands, and for a season the wandering doctor is famous and sought after, lodged among the great. It is one of the very few of his books to be printed while he lives — the harvest of thirty years of battlefields and mines and plague-towns, the surgery of a man who learned his craft from the executioner and the barber. The nobles court him now; but fame keeps him no better than exile did, and soon he is on the road once more.
suggested_refs: Die grosse Wundarznei (Augsburg, 1536), the Great Surgery Book

segments.name: The Return and the White Horse

stops.name: Eferding and Kromau — the Astronomia Magna
stops.campa: In Moravia and at Eferding by the Danube he writes the last and greatest of his philosophies, the Astronomia Magna, the whole book of the greater and the lesser world — how man the microcosm answers star for star to the heavens, how the same wisdom shines in the firmament and in the human soul, how the true adept reads the one in the other. Here he sets down his vision entire: that all knowledge is one, that heaven and earth and the body of man are a single book written in a single hand, and that the physician who would heal must learn to read the whole of it.
stops.quote: Man is a microcosm, or a little world, because he is an extract from all the stars and planets of the whole firmament, from the earth and the elements; and so he is their quintessence.
suggested_refs: Paracelsus's Astronomia Magna, his great book of the microcosm and macrocosm

stops.name: Villach — the return to the father's grave
stops.campa: He comes back at last to Villach in Carinthia, where his father lies buried and his boyhood was spent among the mines. Here he writes his Carinthian works and dedicates the book of miners' diseases to the land that first taught it to him, and offers his philosophy to the estates of the province in gratitude. They praise him and promise to print his books, and do not. Old now and worn by thirty years of roads, he turns his face toward Salzburg, the city that once drove him out — as if a wandering thing, feeling its end, must return to the ground where its trouble began.
suggested_refs: The Carinthian writings, dedicated to the province of his father's grave
sources: Von der Bergsucht (De morbis fossorum metallicorum)

stops.name: Salzburg — recalled under Prince-Archbishop Ernst
stops.campa: The prince-archbishop Ernst of Bavaria, who loves the hidden arts and the alchemist's fire, calls the old doctor back to Salzburg — the very city that drove him out sixteen years before over the peasants' cause. Under a great man's protection at last, Theophrastus comes to rest where his wandering began its exile, and the wheel of his life closes. He is worn and often sick now, his body wasted, some say, by the mercury of his own furnaces, the healer poisoned by the medicine he made. But he is honoured, and he practices, and the citizens of Salzburg see the Monarch of Physicians walk their streets.
suggested_refs: Prince-Archbishop Ernst of Bavaria, who recalled Paracelsus to Salzburg in 1540

stops.name: Salzburg — the White Horse Inn and the last testament
stops.campa: Called back to Salzburg under the protection of the prince-archbishop, Ernst of Bavaria, he takes a small room at the inn Zum Weissen Rössl, the White Horse, on the Kaigasse under the fortress rock. There, felled by a stroke on the twenty-first of September, he dictates his testament: what little he has to his kin at Einsiedeln and to a few Salzburg friends, and all the rest to the poor of the city, for whom he lived and among whom he will lie. The tradition whispers he was struck down by hirelings of the physicians who hated him — the schools' last blow at the man who burned their books.
suggested_refs: The White Horse Inn (Zum Weissen Rössl) on the Kaigasse in Salzburg, where he died

stops.name: St Sebastian's cemetery — the grave among the poor
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of September he dies, forty-seven years old, and is laid as he wished in the paupers' ground of St Sebastian, among the poor he served without fee. The wandering is over; the man who called every land his home and no city his own is given at last a single square of earth. Two centuries later his bones are moved into the church porch and a pyramid of marble raised over them, carved with the promise that his art poured out to the poor what it drew from the world — the wound at his life's root healed into the legend of the Monarch of Physicians.
stops.quote: Alterius non sit qui suus esse potest. — Let no man belong to another who can belong to himself.
stops.quote_source: Motto inscribed on the Hirschvogel portrait of Paracelsus, 1538
suggested_refs: The tomb of Paracelsus at St Sebastian's church, Salzburg, and his motto 'Alterius non sit qui suus esse potest'
sources: 'Alterius non sit qui suus esse potest' (Wikipedia)
